newsitem.title: UK: IRA-a force steeped in anti-British history.
newsitem.headline: IRA-a force steeped in anti-British history.

text.p: The gunmen and bomb experts of the IRA see themselves as standard bearers of an anti-British war that has raged for generations on the island of Ireland.
Insurrection is in the genes of countless fighters who have inherited a determination to break what they regard as a British colonial stranglehold on Northern Ireland imposed several centuries ago.

But they came face to face with the hard fact that some 900,000 Protestants there, comprising a 60 per cent majority, support British rule and refuse to be dragooned into the guerrillas' idea of a "United Ireland".
Moderate Catholic nationalists, and hardline Protestant "Unionists", say the IRA's "freedom fighting" methods have only deepened sectarian divisions.

Protestants in Northern Ireland were reared in families that idolised the British Royal Family, even when it was losing public esteem in mainland Britain. Their menfolk joined the British Army and the province's police force.

IRA attacks over the past 28 years have resulted in hundreds of funerals in Protestant areas, with police guards of honour marching behind the coffins of fellow officers who were blown to pieces or gunned down in street ambushes.

Protestants see the IRA as fighting a sectarian war to crush their British identity and submerge them in an all-Ireland state that would be dominated by the Catholics of the neighbouring Irish Republic and the province's 40 per cent nationalist minority.
Nationalists in Northern Ireland say that from the time when the island was partitioned nearly 80 years ago, the province was run as "a Protestant state for a Protestant people".

Anti-British feeling harboured by nationalists cut off from the rest of Ireland when it gained independence in a 1919-21 Anglo-Irish war intensified because Catholics said they suffered bias in allocation of public housing and jobs.

Every decade since Partition, the IRA has emerged from the shadows but it was in 1969, when a civil rights movement seeking better treatment for Catholics came under violent attack from Protestants, that it surfaced as a new cohesive fighting force.
The Irish Republican Army says it carries the mantle of "United Irishmen", a group of Protestant and Catholic radicals who rose against British rule in 1798 (correct).

The aim of the Society of United Irishmen, who swore secret oaths to resist British rule and who were hanged, flogged or died in battle for their beliefs, was to unite "Catholic, Protestant and Dissenter".
For centuries the Irish saw the British as land-grabbers who were determined to secure the island against any threat that it could be a back-door launch pad for foreign invasion against Britain.
Agrarian agitation in the 1800s led to the formation of a succession of clandestine groups whose hot-headedness grew into acts of open violence against the state.
"Fenian" guerrillas, who were the precursors of the IRA, set off bombs in London in the last century.
Irish hatred of Britain festered further during the 1840s "Great Hunger", a famine that claimed more than a million lives and forced countless hundreds of thousands into emigration.
They blamed Britain for doing nothing to ease the plight of the starving Irish when their staple potato crop failed.
The Famine still haunts the Irish psyche and feeds anti-British sentiment among some hardliners.
